extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of humor/comedy theory, literary critics, playwrights and serious practitioners of comic art
extracted.subtask_description: Analytic theory of the comic: criteria and mechanisms by which things, gestures, social forms and situations become laughable; aimed at explaining/parsing comic effects for criticism or creation. Draws on examples from theatre, literature, social life and everyday observation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic as opposition to gracefulness (rigidness over ugliness)
rubrics_metrics.description: The comic arises when the 'soul' (immaterial gracefulness) that shapes matter is thwarted by matter's obstinacy, producing petrified movements, permanent grimaces and other rigidities; the comic 'partakes rather of the unsprightly than of the unsightly, of RIGIDNESS rather than of UGLINESS.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for situations where life’s suppleness is arrested by material resistance: fixed expressions, stiff postures, mechanical occupations imposed on living motion. These produce comic effect even when not strictly 'ugly.' Examples/explanation in the text: matter dulls outward life of the soul; the result is comic. Anti-pattern: mere ugliness or deformity that does not imply arrested, mechanical motion may not be comic under this rubric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attitudes/gestures laughable in proportion as they suggest a machine
rubrics_metrics.description: THE ATTITUDES, GESTURES AND MOVEMENTS OF THE HUMAN BODY ARE LAUGHABLE IN EXACT PROPORTION AS THAT BODY REMINDS US OF A MERE MACHINE.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate drawings, actors, speakers by how clearly and subtly they enable us to see a person as a jointed puppet — clarity (we must distinctly perceive a mechanism) and subtlety (the person must still appear living) both increase the comic. Example: comic artists who make figures look like puppets without full caricature. Scoring note: the strongest comic effects both suggest internal mechanism and retain an impression of life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition and automatism cause laughter
rubrics_metrics.description: A movement that is always the same, returning at regular intervals, makes us laugh because it evokes a machine that works automatically; repetition implies automatism and is therefore comic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In evaluating a comic bit, check for periodic, expectable gestures or lines that deaden spontaneity; if the audience waits for the recurrence and laughs upon its fulfilment, the comic arises from perceived automatism. Examples: a public speaker whose repeated head/arm motion diverts attention; comic devices on stage like periodical repetition of a word or scene.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation exposes automatism and increases comic effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Gestures that were not laughable become laughable when imitated because imitation highlights the mechanical uniformity — we become imitable only when we cease to be ourselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parody and mimicry work because they bring out the uniform, repeatable elements of a person's behaviour; when assessing parody, look for how it isolates mechanically uniform movements and connects them to simple operations (see mechanical interpretation). Example: imitation that deflects gestures toward sawing wood or striking an anvil increases laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanical interpretation/associating gestures with simple operations
rubrics_metrics.description: Deflecting gestures (without altering their form) toward a mechanical occupation (sawing wood, striking an anvil, tugging a bell-rope) intensifies the sense of mechanism and so the comic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a device, parody should suggest a straightforward mechanical occupation to make the gesture seem intentionally mechanical. This is one 'favourite device of parody' per text. Anti-pattern: mere vulgarity does not equal comic; it's the mechanical association that matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Similarity/uniformity among people (marionette/synchronisation effect)
rubrics_metrics.description: When multiple people simultaneously adopt the same attitudes and movements, we think of marionettes or invisible threads linking them; absolute uniformity stiffens perceived litheness into automatism and provokes laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess group choreography, chorus scenes or ensemble acting for synchronisation that suggests manufactured sameness. The more actors resemble mechanical copies, the stronger the comic. Example: stage groups dancing/gesticulating in unison evoke marionette imagery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot and stage devices revealing clockwork arrangement
rubrics_metrics.description: Devices such as periodical repetition of a word/scene, systematic inversion of parts, and geometrical development of misunderstandings derive comic force from making human events seem like an obvious clockwork arrangement while preserving outward probability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When critiquing or constructing farce, judge how clearly the underlying mechanism of the plot is displayed while still allowing the scene to appear plausible. The playwright’s art is to expose the mechanism without losing a sense of life; success increases comic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disguise, fashion and discontinuity awaken latent comic
rubrics_metrics.description: Fashion, costume or disguise becomes laughable when discontinuity or anachronism makes the covering distinguishable from the person — a sudden dissolution of continuity reveals a previously latent comic quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check whether clothing or fashion is presented so that it draws attention to itself (e.g., a top hat on an eccentric dressed in former times). Continuity of custom dulls comic sense; a break (dressing out of fashion, surprising colour) revives the comic. Example: seeing an old-fashioned dress as a disguise produces laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imagination treats inherent features as artificial (disguise transferred)
rubrics_metrics.description: Even features intrinsic to a person (skin colour, a red nose) can be perceived as a disguise by imagination (as if daubed with ink or vermilion), and thus acquire comic quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing jokes about appearance, note whether the comic effect depends on a mental translation of inherent traits into 'painted' or 'laid-on' features. Historical/ethical caution: the text uses dated racial examples to explain mechanism — treat such examples critically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ceremony and formula become comic when separated from purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Ceremonial forms and official formulas, once isolated in imagination from their serious object, lose seriousness and become comic — 'ceremonies are to the social body what clothing is to the individual body.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate contexts (prize-givings, court sittings, official etiquette) for whether attention is fixed on form over substance. The more the audience thinks only of the form, the more comic the situation becomes. Example: prize-distribution, solemn court scenes rendered absurd by focusing on ritual instead of matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative/regulatory automatism (profession as machine)
rubrics_metrics.description: Officials and professions acting like machines — performing duties by rote or applying rules inexorably — produce a particular comic of pedantry and mechanisation (e.g., asking 'anything to declare' after a shipwreck).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In satire or critique, look for behaviour where means substitute for ends and rules dominate reality. The comic intensifies when professional formality overrides human circumstance. Example: medical/legal characters in Molière whose adherence to form is laughable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical intrusion into moral/emotional context
rubrics_metrics.description: ANY INCIDENT IS COMIC THAT CALLS OUR ATTENTION TO THE PHYSICAL IN A PERSON WHEN IT IS THE MORAL SIDE THAT IS CONCERNED — e.g., a sneeze in a pathetic speech, 'He was virtuous and plump.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess scenes of pathos or moral seriousness for abrupt bodily reminders (sneezes, discomfort, bodily needs) that shift attention from soul to body and thereby provoke laughter. Dramatic anti-pattern: tragic scenes must avoid actions that recall the body (sitting, eating) to preserve tragic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manner seeking to outdo matter (form triumphing over spirit)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy often targets cases where manner, form or procedure seeks to outdo or replace matter, purpose or spirit — 'the manner seeking to outdo the matter, the letter aiming at ousting the spirit.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When constructing or judging comic portrayals of professions, institutions or rituals, look for inversion where the visible form becomes an end in itself (e.g., lawyers/magistrates more concerned with procedure than justice). This is a prime source of professional ridicule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical defects as overtones of intellectual or professional ossification
rubrics_metrics.description: A comic 'fundamental note' (appearance seeking to triumph over reality) tends to be completed by 'overtones' such as bodily defects (stammering, stuttering, slow speech) which echo and prepare the audience to perceive intellectual rigidity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate character construction for the pairing of physical oddities with moral or intellectual flaws — e.g., slow speech accompanying pedantry — as an instinctive device to reinforce comic effect. Note: the pairing functions often unconsciously to prepare the audience for ridicule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Person-as-thing: laughter when a person appears to be a thing
rubrics_metrics.description: WE LAUGH EVERY TIME A PERSON GIVES US THE IMPRESSION OF BEING A THING — e.g., Sancho Panza as a football, clowns becoming bundles or rubber balls, performers becoming wooden dummies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess slapstick and clowning for gradual or sudden transformation imagery where human bodies are pictured as inanimate objects; the more convincingly the sequence leads imagination from living form to thing, the stronger the comic. Examples include circus routines of falling/colliding and exaggerated rebound rhythms that suggest balls or dummies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gradual suggestion/solidification method to produce comic transformation
rubrics_metrics.description: A method of producing comic effect is the gradual passing from vague to distinct suggestion — lulling imagination then increasingly defining the object so that persons seem to solidify into things; poets may use rhythm, rhyme and assonance to lull imagination into accepting the suggested vision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing or crafting comic passages, consider pacing and graduated suggestion: start with dim, fluid images and slowly fix them into a grotesque object to achieve stronger laughter. Examples: hypnotic gradual suggestion and poetic devices that rock imagination between like and like to prepare acceptance of the comic hallucination.
